title: Level generation
thesis: A generated level is worth having only if its shape creates decisions the player can read, and the talks converge on getting there by structure before detail: a plan or graph, authored pieces where human judgement matters, and validation passes that guarantee the level can be finished. Variety is not the goal in itself; a designer should decide what each level is for, what scale and movement it must serve, and which few large axes make one level feel different from the next.

sections.heading: What a generated level is for
sections.brief: Open with the case for generating levels at all: Brian Walker and Herbert Wolverson converge that random levels move the skill curve from memorising routes to mastering systems (Uo9-IcHhq_w#0, TlLIOgWYVpI#0). Then argue that a layout only matters if it creates decisions: John Harris warns that unchallenging contents make the layout meaningless, Walker's combinatorially overlapping zones, Loren Schmidt's idea that players 'read' terrain like a Go board, and Sersa Victory's call to layer several kinds of choice into one encounter all say space is a field of choices, and Harris's Casino Dungeon shows layout itself as a hint. Set this against the counter-position that simple can be right: Tom Francis's deliberately boring Heat Signature levels (structure as chunked progress toward an objective, intricate gates as a chore), Hoplite's near-trivial generator, and Oliver Withington's point that only the designer knows what diversity the generator needs. End with Alexander Birke's guidance to understand the pattern you are generating and where you can cheat, as the first question to ask before writing a generator.

sections.heading: Fitting space to the game's rules and scale
sections.brief: Argue that level geometry is not neutral: it must suit how the game moves, sees and is played. Start with movement and grids: Walker's defence of square grids with one-step diagonals, Chogue's two-wide corridors for bishops, Wildermyth's large monsters stuck in narrow procedural passages, Into Ruins dropping doors because they touch FOV, AI and pathing, and NetHack corridors that defeated a blind-accessible description (Alexei Pepers). Then scale: platformer and multiplayer designers (Tyriq Plummer twice) converge on small, dense stages, Slashie on a smaller region packed with discoveries, Jon Perry on capping Mini and Max's nested scales, while Plummer and Moria's history defend the pull of vast space. Set Sunless Sea's deliberately slow ship and Animal-Crossing-like bounded space against Todd Furmanski's abstract point-of-interest travel and HyperRogue's infinite hyperbolic world, and use Everest Pipkin's account of why enclosed underground space naturally divides into directional rooms. End with guidance: size and shape levels from movement rules, run length and player count, not from what the generator can produce.

sections.heading: Handcrafted and procedural: where to draw the line
sections.brief: This is the chapter's central decision. Lead with the strongest convergence in the pack: many teams found authored pieces assembled procedurally beat fully generated space. Sebastien Benard's Dead Cells rooms (cheap to draw, purposeful, generation of platforms failed because gravity makes jumps asymmetric), Darius Kazemi's analysis of Spelunky's 60-70% fixed templates whose sameness lets players learn rhythm, Sergio Garces's hundred hand-authored layouts, NetHack's special levels (Jesse Collet) and level compilers, and Alexei Pepers's advice to snap together chunks. Then the 'hand-made feel' argument: Ben Berman wants generated levels to look hand-made, via symmetry (Binding of Isaac) and by rejecting difficulty as the parameter. Stage the disagreement over the seam: Jon Perry stopped hiding it in Mini and Max because constraining handcrafted areas to match procgen made them worse, while Wildermyth's team weighs cheap procedural maps against special handcrafted ones. Cover practical patterns (probabilistic tiles, tag-based room pools, separating layout from dressing as Dead Cells, Diablo and Garces do, toggled authored layers in Prey: Mooncrash) and end with the 80/20 maxim and a guide for choosing the ratio.

sections.heading: Layout algorithms and how to combine them
sections.brief: A technical tour specific enough to implement from, organised by family rather than by talk. Start with the history (Rogue's 3x3 'tic-tac-toe' grid, described by Michael Toy, John Harris and Mark Gritter) and the beginner's room placement, then rooms-and-corridors (BSP with a gutter, Spencer Egart's BSP plus prefab rooms plus A* hallways, Trogue's rewrite-rule corridors), organic carving (cellular automata with Wolverson's neighbour thresholds, drunkard's walk, DLA, random-walk stampers, 3D CA caves in Rite of Tephra), and Brogue's room accretion. Give parameters wherever the speakers did. Then make the key argument: Wolverson (w3) and Tyler Coleman converge that you rarely need just one technique and that combining them can tell a story; Brian Bucklew's WFC pre-pass/post-pass and Desktop Dungeons' recipes of events to swappable handlers are two architectures for doing it. End with generate-and-test (Emoji Meadow's discarded paths) and a short decision guide: which family suits which kind of space.

sections.heading: Giving the generator a plan: graphs, loops and set pieces
sections.brief: Argue that good levels need structure above the tile level. Joris Dormans says the generator needs a plan, and graph-based approaches converge across talks: Unexplored's mission and space split (relayed by Abdelrahman Madkour), Ian Holmes's graph grammars and guaranteed cyclic shortcuts, Dormans's multi-pass generation and backward planning from the final dragon, Dead Cells' node tree, and Wolverson's hot path for culling or rewarding off-path areas. Add Brian Walker's structural fixes on a skeleton: loops added where path distance is long, choke-point analysis, and machines specified as minimal qualitative relationships that interlock across a level into concrete goals. Add Jack Schlesinger's dramatic arc of tension and release as the shape a plan should take. Close with the counterweight: Dormans's warning that generating everything in advance makes fragile machines that collapse when the player deviates, so plan space more than time.

sections.heading: Guaranteeing a playable level
sections.brief: How to make sure every generated level can be finished, and that being stuck is fair. Begin with the definition from Jack Schlesinger: no inaccessible rooms and no unintentional dead ends. Then techniques that converge on flood fills and pathfinding: Wolverson's Dijkstra culling, Bucklew's A* door punching with high wall weight and noise-guided cave passages, Walker's placement checks for lakes and his 'wells of doom' fix for platformers, Spelunky's room-connection rules. Then lock-and-key and item gating: Stella Mazeika's circular-dependency warning, Jon Perry's Planet Zoldath (stable item core, multiple solutions per gate, never keys behind their own gate) and hidden guidance funnels, and procedural metroidvania backtracking. Finish with recovery: Unexplored's 'pray for help' stuck check, plus Schlesinger's caution about locally correct moves that cascade into unsolvability. End with a checklist-style In practice list of validation passes.

sections.heading: Furnishing and populating the layout
sections.brief: Once the shape exists, where do things go? Organise by technique: measuring the space (Albert Ford's FOV-based openness for caves, Wolverson's Dijkstra 'least accessible point' for hidden bonuses, Voronoi cells to keep monster groups together or apart), placing threats (Shattered Pixel Dungeon's per-floor enemy deck, Emily Halina's TRP placing the most impactful threat first, lairs in Rift Wizard and Alphaman), and furnishing rooms (Pierre Vigier's constraint-satisfaction rooms with margin cells and a required/optional split, and Stream Heist's hand-authored placement slots spread with heat maps). Include placed stories and hazards: NetHack's trap-killed adventurers, Reed Lockwood's traps that reshape the dungeon, and The Banished Vault's mutually exclusive resource tiles. End with the common guidance that populating needs its own rules about spacing, fairness and access, not just random scatter.

sections.heading: Making levels distinct and memorable
sections.brief: The oatmeal problem applied to levels: a generator that produces endless variation can still produce sameness. Lead with Rich Wilson's 'chopped salad effect' from Prey: Mooncrash (one dominant hazard per level rather than a little of everything) and set it beside Sea of Rifts' per-harbor prop weight ranges and Angband's boring uniform deep levels; these converge on chunkier variation. Then tools for standout levels: Isaac Karth's landmarks, contrast between levels and asking what makes one level stand out, No Man's Sky's single biome per planet, and Wildermyth's scenery by biome and enemy type mattering more than shape variation; Garces's cap on repeated prefabs per screen and Sea of Rifts' per-biome scenery rules are the dressing-level version. Then meaning: John Harris's argument that hand-made dungeons have a backstory that players can exploit, and Mike Cook's point that a generator expresses itself differently as content changes across worlds. End with guidance: vary along few large axes, give each level an identity players can name, and let content context do work the layout cannot.

sections.heading: Mazes, orientation and getting lost
sections.brief: A focused section, mostly from Andrew Plotkin's talk, on when confusing space is the point. Start with his definition: a maze is an experience, marked by the intent to get you lost, and a good maze lets the player reorient through effort rather than simply disorienting them (w3). Set this against roguelike practice: grid maze algorithms that guarantee connectivity, John Harris's perfect versus imperfect mazes (Larn's multiple routes give choices), Noah Swartz's reading of twisting levels as there to slow and befuddle, and mapping as part of the maze experience. Include construction details: Todd Furmanski's quadrant placement and dummy rooms in Dragon's Descent, Adrian Herbez's bit-flag cells, and Plotkin's ways to defeat the left-hand rule. End with guidance on including mazes for their own pleasure, not just for difficulty.

sections.heading: Between levels: doors, branches and the run's route
sections.brief: How levels join into a run. Lead with Rosalind Miles Chapman's argument that modern roguelikes replace the hunger clock with mutually exclusive path choices, making a push-your-luck decision explicit, and Moria's town level (Santiago Zapata) as the first structural break from a pure dive. Use John Bond's taxonomy of 'doors' (linear, dungeon doors, chosen doors, branching map, open world) and his four variables (run length, pacing, number of major mechanics, polish) as the frame, with Casey Yano's account of why Slay the Spire needed a map and Sersa Victory's and Rift Wizard's previewable choices. Then NetHack's branches and Vlad's Tower breaking level independence, Into Ruins' holes and Chogue's party transitions, Angband's non-persistent levels, Noita's clash between seamless worlds and static transition rooms, and data on branch difficulty from Crawl. End with guidance for choosing a door system by run shape.

sections.heading: Worlds, overworlds and persistence
sections.brief: Generating at the scale of a world, and deciding what persists. Lead with Caves of Qud's layered approach: a framework generated at world creation (history, roads, villages, lairs) that constrains zones fabricated lazily on entry, the static world map whose tiles expand into 3x3 zones, and history-named locations that become real places. Set Sea of Rifts against layered noise (Birke's warning that noise has no concept of good play; his islands grown from harbors, concentric difficulty zones, jittered-grid cities) and Loren Schmidt's terrain that must work in positive and negative and his flick-screen overworld, with Dwarf Fortress's layered biome map as the classic. Then persistence and seeds: Animal Crossing generating once, Mini and Max's locked seed, Alphaman's position-derived seeds, Dragon's Descent's 12-byte levels, Chronicles of Stampadia's pre-generated dungeon revealed by lookup, Oath's persistent maps, shared multiplayer dungeons and player seed curation. End with when to generate up front, lazily, or once.

sections.heading: Unusual spaces and new inputs
sections.brief: The frontier and edge cases. Start with digging and destructible terrain (Everest Pipkin on digging as old as video games, SteamWorld Dig making getting stuck the core tension, wells as thresholds) as spaces players reshape. Then generators driven by non-traditional inputs: Tyler Coleman's song-driven dungeons with a build-up and boss at the climax, webcam blob detection and texture maps as heightmaps. Then learning and optimisation: Aaron Santos's gradient-descent generators that satisfy only what the loss measures (connectivity, dead ends), a useful warning for any automated tuning. Include Younes Rabii's Pokemon Glitch, where randomly moving tiles sometimes made areas unreachable, Bioloom's vertex-adjacency moon, Minecraft's Far Lands as where a generator's rules fail, and Alexandra Leonhart's reading of procedural generation as 'unworlding'. End with what these experiments suggest for conventional generators.
